content: Gold salts refer to ionic chemical compounds containing gold, although the term is a misnomer. In medical contexts, the term has evolved to describe gold-based compounds used therapeutically. The use of gold compounds in medicine is known as chrysotherapy or aurotherapy. Research into their medical applications began in 1935, primarily focusing on reducing inflammation and slowing disease progression in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis. Despite the name, most gold compounds used in medicine are not true salts. Beyond medicine, gold compounds are also widely used in electroplating and as reagents in organic chemistry. Gold compounds accumulate slowly in the body and are known to reduce inflammation over time. They are particularly effective in treating rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis, membranous nephritis, lupus erythematosus, and, less commonly, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA). The exact mechanism by which gold drugs exert their effects in arthritis remains a topic of scientific debate. It is hypothesized that gold binds to albumin in the bloodstream, with thiol groups on the gold drug exchanging with cysteine residues on albumin. Upon reaching the synovium, gold undergoes further thiol exchange reactions at cell membrane transport proteins and enters cells via a shuttle thiol mechanism. Once inside the cell, gold is thought to interfere with mitochondrial activity and induce apoptosis. However, the non-specific absorption and pharmacological actions of gold compounds can lead to a wide range of side effects, affecting cells unrelated to the immune response in rheumatoid arthritis. Some researchers suggest that gold drugs primarily inhibit immune system components associated with rheumatoid arthritis rather than curing the disease. Gold salts are rarely used in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (formerly juvenile rheumatoid arthritis), as methotrexate is the standard treatment. However, they may be considered for children with progressive polyarthritis unresponsive to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), methotrexate, and other medications. This treatment is costly, requiring frequent doctor visits and numerous laboratory tests. Gold drugs can be administered orally or via intramuscular injection. Intramuscular administration typically involves weekly injections for three to five months, followed by less frequent dosing. Auranofin, an oral gold compound, is marketed under the brand name Ridaura. Regular urine tests to monitor for protein (indicating potential kidney damage) and blood tests are necessary during treatment. A 2005 review by Suarez-Almazor et al. reported that intramuscular gold (parenteral gold) reduces disease activity and joint inflammation. Oral gold salts are less effective than injectable forms. Noticeable symptom improvement often requires three to six months of treatment. A 2002 study by Richards et al. documented neurological side effects of gold salts, with historical evidence suggesting potential efficacy in treating neurological disorders. The authors noted that further research could re-establish gold as a significant therapeutic agent for a broader range of conditions. Side effects of gold salts may develop after significant accumulation in the body. Gold compounds require up to two months to reach a steady state and have a long half-life, with only 70% excreted within 10 days, increasing the risk of toxicity. The potential benefits for patients with inflammatory bowel disease, skin rash, or a history of bone marrow depression must be weighed against the risks of gold toxicity, particularly in compromised organ systems. Detecting and attributing toxic effects accurately can be challenging. Oral gold administration has fewer side effects than intramuscular injections. Common side effects of oral gold include decreased appetite, nausea, hair thinning, and diarrhea, as well as issues affecting the skin, blood, kidneys, or lungs. Injected gold commonly causes itchy skin rashes or mouth sores, with rare cases of kidney problems or suppression of blood cell production. Future research into gold salts has explored their potential as treatments for autism and cancer. Auranofin has demonstrated toxicity toward leukemia cells, and various gold salts under investigation have shown efficacy against cisplatin-resistant cancer cells, suggesting unique mechanisms of action. Gold salts combined with chloroquine, an anti-malarial drug, have shown promise in treating resistant strains of malaria. In Japan, gold salts used for rheumatoid arthritis, particularly gold thioglucose, have been proposed as potential treatments for bronchial asthma. Industrial uses of gold salts, such as in electroplating, carry risks like occupational contact eczema.
